title: 2.1 Linear Algebra — the language of ML
description: Roadmap 2.1 — 14 topics, in the document's own order.
learningOutcomes: Read a matrix as a linear map and predict its geometric effect, rank, and conditioning before computing.
Choose the right factorisation — LU, Cholesky, QR, eigendecomposition, SVD — from the matrix's structure and the numerically safe way to compute it.
Use the SVD and low-rank approximation as the working tools behind PCA, LoRA, and compression.
Run matrix calculus and the chain rule as backpropagation, and reason about FLOPs, arithmetic intensity, and why batching wins.

lessons.title: Vectors, vector spaces, span, basis, dimension, linear independence
lessons.description: Define a vector by the axioms of the space it lives in, then use span, independence, basis, and dimension as the working vocabulary for feature redundancy, embedding size, and the solution set of a linear system — including how each test changes in floating point.
learningObjectives: State the vector space axioms and recognise polynomials, functions, and parameter tensors as vectors
Test a set of vectors for linear independence through the trivial-combination condition and through a tolerant rank
Build a basis for a span, read a vector's coordinates in it, and explain why dimension is well defined
Connect span, rank, and dimension to feature collinearity, embedding width, and underdetermined systems

lessons.title: Matrices as linear transformations (geometric view first, always)
lessons.description: Read a matrix as a function that moves space — its columns are the images of the basis vectors — and use that picture to predict what scaling, rotation, shear, projection, and rank collapse do before touching arithmetic.
learningObjectives: Explain why a linear map is fixed entirely by where it sends a basis, and read a matrix's columns as those images
Classify a 2x2 matrix as scaling, rotation, reflection, shear, or projection from its geometric effect on the unit square
Connect determinant to signed area change and rank to the dimension of the image, including the collapse case
Describe a non-square matrix as a map between spaces of different dimension and relate it to a linear layer

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication — four different mental models of it
lessons.description: The same product AB read four ways — entrywise dot products, A acting on the columns of B, the rows of A acting on B, and a sum of rank-1 outer products — plus why it is really function composition, and which view to reach for when.
learningObjectives: Compute and explain AB through all four views and state which one a given problem makes easy
Justify the shape rule, non-commutativity, associativity, and distributivity from the composition view
Use the outer-product view to see low-rank updates, attention scores, and the gradient of a linear layer
Reason about the cost of a matrix chain and why association order changes the FLOP count

lessons.title: Transpose, inverse, pseudo-inverse, determinant, trace, rank
lessons.description: Six scalar-and-matrix operations that summarise a linear map — what each one measures geometrically, how they relate through the SVD, and which ones you must never compute the naive way in production code.
learningObjectives: Define transpose through the dot product and use it to move a matrix across an inner product
State the exact conditions for an inverse to exist and explain why you solve rather than invert
Derive the pseudo-inverse from the SVD and say what problem it solves when there is no true inverse
Read determinant, trace, and rank as invariants of the map and pick numerically safe ways to compute them

lessons.title: Systems of linear equations, Gaussian elimination, LU decomposition
lessons.description: Solve Ax = b by the row and column pictures, run Gaussian elimination as a sequence of left-multiplications, and store the work as an LU factorisation you reuse across many right-hand sides — with partial pivoting for numerical safety.
learningObjectives: Read a system through both the row picture and the column picture and state when it has zero, one, or many solutions
Run Gaussian elimination as elementary row operations and identify pivots, rank, and free variables
Explain why partial pivoting is needed and what the permutation matrix records
Produce and reuse an LU (or PA = LU) factorisation, and know when Cholesky or QR is the better tool

lessons.title: Inner products, norms (L0/L1/L2/L∞/Frobenius), orthogonality, projections
lessons.description: The inner product defines length and angle; the p-norms measure size in different ways with different unit balls; orthogonality and projection turn "closest point in a subspace" into least squares.
learningObjectives: State the inner product axioms and derive length, angle, and Cauchy-Schwarz from them
Compare the L1, L2, L-infinity, L0, Frobenius, and spectral norms by their unit balls and their uses
Compute projections onto a vector and onto a subspace, and show the residual is orthogonal
Connect norms and projection to weight decay, sparsity, cosine similarity, and least squares

lessons.title: Gram–Schmidt, QR decomposition
lessons.description: Turn any basis into an orthonormal one spanning the same nested subspaces, package that as A = QR, and use it for least squares without the normal equations — with modified Gram-Schmidt and Householder reflections for numerical safety.
learningObjectives: Run classical and modified Gram-Schmidt and explain why the modified version keeps orthogonality
Read A = QR as "orthonormal basis for the column space" plus "the coefficients in R"
Solve least squares through QR and say why it beats forming the normal equations
Compare Gram-Schmidt, Householder, and Givens, and measure loss of orthogonality

lessons.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, eigendecomposition, diagonalisation
lessons.description: The directions a matrix only stretches, the factors it stretches them by, and the change of basis A = V Lambda V-inverse that turns matrix powers, stability questions, and PCA into scalar arithmetic.
learningObjectives: Define an eigenpair and read A = V Lambda V-inverse as "change to the eigenbasis, scale, change back"
Use the eigendecomposition to compute matrix powers, decide A^k convergence, and read trace and determinant
Distinguish diagonalisable from defective matrices and algebraic from geometric multiplicity
Explain why the characteristic polynomial is the wrong numerical route and when to use eig versus eigh

lessons.title: Symmetric matrices, positive (semi-)definiteness — critical for optimisation
lessons.description: Symmetric matrices always diagonalise orthogonally; the sign of their quadratic form splits bowls from saddles, decides convexity, and determines whether Newton, conjugate gradient, Cholesky, and a covariance estimate will work at all.
learningObjectives: Apply the spectral theorem and read the quadratic form x·Ax as an ellipsoid, saddle, or dome
Test positive definiteness four ways and pick the cheapest definitive one
Connect PSD Hessians to convexity and PD Hessians to a well-posed Newton step
Repair a matrix that should be PSD but is not, and know why kernels and covariances must be PSD

lessons.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) — the single most useful decomposition in ML
lessons.description: Every matrix factors as a rotation, an axis-aligned scaling, and another rotation; the scaling factors are the singular values, and reading them gives you rank, norms, conditioning, the pseudo-inverse, PCA, and the best low-rank approximation.
learningObjectives: State A = U Sigma V-transpose for any matrix and describe the rotate-scale-rotate geometry it encodes
Relate singular values and vectors to the eigendecomposition of A-transpose-A and A-A-transpose
Read rank, the four fundamental subspaces, the spectral/Frobenius/nuclear norms, and the condition number off the SVD
Explain why the SVD is the numerically safe tool and when a truncated or randomized SVD is used

lessons.title: Low-rank approximation — this is literally what LoRA is
lessons.description: When a matrix's singular values decay fast, a few rank-1 terms reproduce it almost exactly; that is compression, PCA, and — with a frozen base weight plus a trained rank-r update — LoRA.
learningObjectives: Use Eckart-Young to build the optimal rank-k approximation and quantify its error from the tail of the spectrum
Convert a low-rank factorisation into concrete storage and FLOP savings
Write out LoRA as W0 + BA and explain the initialisation, the scaling, and the inference merge
Decide from the singular value spectrum whether a matrix is worth approximating at low rank

lessons.title: Matrix calculus: Jacobians, gradients, the layout conventions, chain rule for matrices
lessons.description: Derivatives when the inputs and outputs are vectors and matrices — the gradient and Jacobian shapes, a layout convention to keep them straight, the standard identities, and the chain rule that is exactly backpropagation.
learningObjectives: Give the shape of the gradient and Jacobian for scalar-by-vector, scalar-by-matrix, and vector-by-vector derivatives, under a stated layout
Apply the standard identities for d(Ax), d(x-transpose-A-x), d(tr(AX)), and d(log det X)
Run the chain rule as a product of Jacobians and recognise it as reverse-mode backprop via vector-Jacobian products
Derive the gradients of a linear layer and a softmax, and verify any gradient with a finite-difference check

lessons.title: Tensors: what they actually are vs. what PyTorch calls them
lessons.description: The mathematical tensor is a multilinear object with a transformation law; the "tensor" in a deep learning framework is an n-dimensional array with a dtype and a stride layout. Knowing which one you mean clarifies einsum, contraction, and tensor decompositions.
learningObjectives: Contrast the mathematical tensor (multilinear map with a change-of-basis law) with the framework tensor (typed strided array)
Express batched matmul, attention, and bilinear layers as einsum contractions and reason about contraction order
Describe an n-d array as a flat buffer plus shape and strides, and predict when permute and reshape copy
Explain what CP, Tucker, and Kronecker factorisations generalise from the matrix SVD and where they are used

lessons.title: Computational cost: FLOPs of matmul, memory layout, why batching wins
lessons.description: Count the FLOPs of the matmuls in a model, use arithmetic intensity and the roofline to tell compute-bound from memory-bound, and see why batching turns a memory-bound matrix-vector product into a compute-bound matrix-matrix one.
learningObjectives: Count the FLOPs of a matmul and of the main layers of a transformer, and use the 2 x params x tokens rule
Compute arithmetic intensity and place an operation on the roofline as compute- or memory-bound
Explain why a row-major layout, contiguity, and cache blocking matter, and what BLAS level 3 buys
Show quantitatively why batching amortises the weight load and moves a matvec into the compute-bound regime
